query: W melts near 3422 °C, whereas Cu boils near 2562 °C, so conventional induction or arc-plasma casting cannot readily yield a uniform W–Cu material. Phase separation and void formation can impair thermal transport. Filling a W skeleton with molten Cu or Cu powder can leave defects; spark-plasma sintering and mechanical alloying can produce finer, more uniform structures but can also leave voids; vapor-coated W powders have been sintered to achieve near-perfect contact between the constituents; and metal 3D printing has also been explored. Starting from W particles or connected W regions within a Cu matrix for heat transfer under irradiation in fusion-reactor joints, what single intervention could overcome these limitations while preserving mechanical durability? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention and mechanism, predicts an outcome relative to a named existing fabrication baseline, defines the processing and service boundaries, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment and observations that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Conformal deposition of a nanometric copper layer (≈20–50 nm) on every tungsten surface by atomic-layer deposition (ALD) prior to field-assisted sintering will eliminate nearly all inter-particle voids and markedly strengthen Cu-W bonding.  Relative to a baseline spark-plasma–sintered (SPS) composite made from the same W and Cu powders without the ALD step, the coated-powder route will (i) cut the residual interfacial void fraction below 0.5 vol % and (ii) raise the room-temperature effective thermal conductivity by ≥15 % while keeping the compressive strength within ±5 % of the baseline after 10⁵ thermal cycles between 25 °C and 1000 °C under a fusion-relevant 14 MeV neutron dose of 5 dpa.
generation.material_initial_state: High-purity spherical W powders (5–20 µm) mechanically mixed with dendritic Cu powders (1–5 µm); optional pre-compacted open-porosity W skeletons (>15 vol % connected porosity).
generation.intervention: Atomic-layer deposition of Cu to a thickness of 20–50 nm on every exposed W surface before consolidation (single, well-controlled ALD cycle sequence using Cu(I)(hfac)(tmvs) precursor with H₂ plasma reduction).
generation.conditions: Field-assisted spark-plasma sintering at 950 °C, 50 MPa, 10 min hold in 10⁻² Pa Ar, followed by service in a He-cooled fusion divertor joint: 25–1000 °C cyclic temperature, 1 MPa mechanical stress, and 5 dpa neutron exposure.
generation.structural_mediator: Conformal, oxide-free Cu nano-film at every W–Cu and W–W contact that sinters/diffuses into the bulk Cu phase during SPS, providing a continuous metallic path and healing nano-scale gaps.
generation.mechanism: The pre-laid Cu nanolayer (1) acts as a fast-diffusing transient liquid/solid phase during the initial current pulses, filling surface asperities by capillary flow; (2) removes tungsten-oxide barriers via in-situ reduction; (3) enlarges the metallurgical contact area, suppressing Kirkendall porosity; and (4) converts to bulk Cu, leaving a dense, continuous Cu network that bridges W domains and maintains ductility under irradiation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared with uncoated-powder SPS specimens, ALD-coated materials will show: • ≤0.5 % interfacial voids (X-ray tomography); • ≥265 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹ room-T effective thermal conductivity (vs. 230 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹ baseline); • ≥950 MPa compressive yield strength, retained to ≥900 MPa after 10⁵ thermal cycles; • No new interfacial cracking after 5 dpa, as verified by TEM.
generation.baseline: Spark-plasma–sintered W–Cu composite made from the same un-coated mixed powders, consolidated under identical SPS parameters.
generation.boundary: Valid only for W volume fractions 50–80 %, Cu layer thickness 10–100 nm, sintering temperatures ≤1100 °C, and neutron doses ≤5 dpa; ALD must yield >95 % conformality and <1 at % impurity.
generation.uncertainty: Scaling ALD to kilogram-scale powder lots and ensuring complete coverage in deep, tortuous porosity remain non-trivial; irradiation-assisted Cu diffusion or radiation-induced segregation at W|Cu could degrade interfaces long-term.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets (n ≥ 5 each) of cylindrical specimens (10 mm × 10 mm): (A) baseline SPS from un-coated powders, (B) ALD-Cu–coated W powders SPS-consolidated identically. Characterize density and voids by Archimedes and µ-CT, measure thermal diffusivity (laser flash) and calculate conductivity (density & specific heat). Conduct compressive tests at RT and after 10⁵ thermal cycles (25↔1000 °C, 5 min dwell, He atmosphere). Irradiate half of each set to 5 dpa at 550 °C in a fission reactor, then repeat tests and TEM cross-section imaging.
measurements: Compressive yield strength before/after thermal cycling
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: Hypothesis is falsified if ANY of the following hold with 95 % confidence: (1) Mean void fraction of set B exceeds 0.5 vol % or is not at least 50 % lower than set A; (2) Thermal conductivity improvement of set B over set A is <10 % at any temperature; (3) Compressive yield strength of set B is >5 % lower than set A either before or after cycling; (4) TEM shows interfacial crack density in set B ≥ set A after irradiation.
